A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the quantitative measurement of p53 protein by immunoassay is superior to qualitative assessment of p53 status by immunohistochemistry in identifying non‐small cell carcinoma patients with increased risk of relapsing and dying.
we have shown that the p53 protein level in lung cancer extracts is a strong prognostic marker for disease relapse and death in patients with non‐small cell carcinoma.
the p53 concentration measured in the tumour tissue is a significant predictor of survival for patients with NSCLC.
The main takeaway from our work is that
p53 protein concentration is an independent predictor of relapse and survival in non‐small lung cancer patients.
p53 protein levels in lung cancer are prognostic of survival, and that the impact of high p53 levels on survival is greater for squamous cell carcinoma compared to adenocarcinomas.
p53 protein levels in lung cancer are prognostically significant, but not in the same way that p53 gene mutations are prognostically important.
